clinicalPearls: Classically affects young adult men, typically presenting with sudden painless loss of vision or floaters from vitreous haemorrhage rather than from the underlying vasculitis itself.
The disease is an idiopathic obliterative peripheral retinal periphlebitis; venous involvement predominates over arterial, distinguishing it from many other retinal vasculitides.
Diagnosis is one of exclusion, made only after systemic and infective causes of retinal vasculitis have been actively ruled out.
A strong association with hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein is recognised, particularly in the Indian subcontinent, though active systemic tuberculosis is usually absent.

The natural history progresses through three overlapping phases: active periphlebitis, peripheral retinal capillary non-perfusion (ischaemia), and neovascularisation with its haemorrhagic complications.
Fundus fluorescein angiography is central to management, delineating the extent of peripheral capillary non-perfusion and areas of leakage that guide laser photocoagulation.
Bilateral involvement is common though often asymmetrical, so the fellow eye must always be examined and monitored even when asymptomatic.
Corticosteroids control the inflammatory (vasculitic) phase while sectoral or scatter laser photocoagulation addresses the ischaemic and neovascular phases.
reference.pathophysiology: Eales disease is an idiopathic inflammatory occlusive vasculopathy centred on the peripheral retinal veins. An initial perivascular inflammatory infiltrate (periphlebitis) causes vessel wall thickening, sheathing and progressive luminal occlusion. The resulting peripheral capillary non-perfusion generates retinal ischaemia, which upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor and drives the formation of fragile retinal and optic disc neovascular tufts. These new vessels bleed readily into the vitreous, producing the characteristic recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, and later fibrovascular proliferation may exert tractional forces leading to retinal detachment. A delayed hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial (tuberculoprotein) antigen is strongly implicated as a trigger of the immune-mediated vascular injury in predisposed individuals, alongside proposed roles for oxidative stress and altered retinal autoimmunity, but no single causative organism is consistently demonstrated within the affected tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Tuberculous retinal vasculitis with active systemic infection
Behcet disease with occlusive retinal vasculitis
Sickle cell (and other haemoglobinopathy) proliferative retinopathy
Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease
additionalInvestigations: Fundus fluorescein angiography to map capillary non-perfusion and neovascular leakage
B-scan ultrasonography when vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundus, to exclude retinal detachment
Tuberculin skin testing or interferon-gamma release assay
Chest imaging to screen for pulmonary tuberculosis or sarcoidosis
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and inflammatory markers
Optical coherence tomography for associated macular oedema
Wide-field retinal imaging to document peripheral involvement over time
redFlags: Sudden marked loss of vision indicating fresh dense vitreous haemorrhage
New floaters or a shadow in the peripheral field suggesting tractional retinal detachment
Neovascularisation of the optic disc, carrying high risk of recurrent bleeding
Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage requiring surgical intervention
Rubeosis iridis or raised intraocular pressure signalling anterior segment neovascularisation
reference.prognosis: With timely laser photocoagulation of ischaemic retina and control of the inflammatory phase, visual prognosis is generally favourable and many eyes retain good vision. Outcomes worsen with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, macular involvement or tractional retinal detachment, though modern vitreoretinal surgery salvages useful vision in a substantial proportion of advanced cases.
pitfalls: Labelling any peripheral retinal vasculitis as Eales disease without first excluding tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and Behcet disease.
Overlooking the asymptomatic fellow eye, which may harbour early treatable periphlebitis or ischaemia.
Attributing painless visual loss solely to the vasculitis and missing an underlying tractional retinal detachment behind vitreous haemorrhage.
Treating the inflammatory phase with corticosteroids while neglecting laser ablation of established peripheral non-perfusion.
Failing to arrange long-term follow-up, so recurrent neovascular bleeding goes undetected until vision is lost.
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Retina and Vitreous
management: Apply laser photocoagulation to ischaemic peripheral retina, guided by fundus fluorescein angiography, to regress neovascularisation and prevent recurrent haemorrhage
Control the active inflammatory periphlebitis phase with corticosteroids, given systemically or by periocular or intravitreal route
Use intravitreal anti-VEGF injection as an adjunct for active neovascularisation or associated macular oedema
Undertake pars plana vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
Investigate for tuberculoprotein hypersensitivity and, where latent tuberculosis is confirmed, consider antituberculous therapy in conjunction with a physician
Arrange regular ophthalmic surveillance for recurrent haemorrhage and neovascular complications in the fellow eye
Coordinate care between ophthalmology and physician or tuberculosis specialist input
